title: Semester Two and New for the Sake of New
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Responding to a reviewer who complained that his book had too little that was new, Stuart argues that teachers do not need new things; they need permission to focus. He offers two reasons for our appetite for novelty: a marketing machine that profits from convincing us we need something new, and impatience with returning to the same sandbox. Because time is the currency teachers are poorest in, he argues, chasing the next initiative costs more than it yields. He then models the alternative by listing a small improvement goal for each of his six focus areas in semester two, from student beliefs and knowledge-building to primary sources and feedback turnaround. The post is a practical case for depth over novelty in teacher improvement, with a printable tracker as the tool.
points: Teachers rarely need new ideas; they need permission to stop chasing novelty and go deeper into a few practices.
Both marketing incentives and personal impatience drive the appetite for the Next Thing, so resisting it takes deliberate effort.
Staying in the same few sandboxes for years, getting slightly better each time, beats rotating through initiatives.
Stuart models semester goals by writing one small, measurable improvement for each of his six focus areas, such as reading 50 primary sources or giving next-day feedback.
New is justified only when what you are doing truly will not work, and focusing also saves the time spent hunting for novelty.
quotes: The answer, of course, is that there's not a ton of new in my book, just like there's not much new on this blog. You and I don't tend to need new — we need permission to focus, permission to jump off the hamster wheel and just think. New for the sake of new is kind of crazy — long-term flourishing is what we're after, not new.

Part of this is probably the marketing machine we're marinating in each day. There's a market incentive for creating new and improved, and so there are advertising dollars and teams of smart people aiming, every day, at getting you and me to buy the idea that what we need is something new, something that we just haven't quite bought yet.

Another reason might be that we're impatient — it's easier to move toward the Next Thing than it is to keep coming back to the same old sandbox. The trouble with our impatience, of course, is that it's so likely to lead us astray. After all, the sandboxes we've been digging in for months or years may just be the ones to camp out in for decades, getting a little bit better at them all the time.

So far, I've been amazed at how much better my students argue when I give them a chance to become knowledgeable on the topic first. I mean, I know that knowing things makes you think better, but it's still just sort of magical to see it happen.

This one's a stretch goal, but I'd love to get my general world history kids to read 50 different primary source documents in semester two. We had to be close to that in semester one, but I did a poor job keeping track of the number.

I'll be writing about these in the months to come, but my point in this post is to push you to resist the undertow toward new. New doesn't make sense unless what we're already doing really, really won't work.
They'll get stronger, and so will I. And think of all the time I'll save not seeking the next big thing to occupy my time and attention. I'll focus, and I'll get better.
